difficultyRationale: Tests understanding of the underlying hash-based structural property behind set membership checks, independent of any specific language's collection library.
prompt: A backend service must repeatedly check, 'have I already processed this order ID?' against a growing collection of millions of previously processed IDs. Considered purely as data structures (not as any particular language's library classes), what is the key structural reason a hash-based set outperforms an unsorted list for this membership-check workload?
explanation: A hash-based set computes a hash of the key to locate the relevant bucket directly, giving average O(1) membership checks regardless of how many elements are stored. An unsorted list has no such shortcut: checking membership requires scanning elements one by one until a match is found or the list ends, which is O(n).

options.text: A hash-based set keeps its elements in sorted order internally, which enables binary search that narrows the candidate range by half with each comparison, the same way it would on a sorted array, while a list cannot be sorted.
options.explanation: A hash-based set is not ordered by key value at all; its bucket placement depends on the hash, not on sort order. Sorted-order lookup with binary search describes a tree-based or sorted-array structure, not a hash-based set.

options.text: A hash-based set stores elements contiguously like an array, so checking membership is just a direct index lookup by position.
options.explanation: A hash-based set does not know an element's bucket index without first computing its hash, and multiple elements can still collide into the same bucket, requiring a secondary comparison step rather than a single direct index lookup.

options.text: A hash-based set computes a hash of the key to jump to the relevant bucket directly, giving average O(1) membership checks, while an unsorted list must scan from the start, giving O(n).
options.explanation: Correct: hashing lets the set locate a small candidate bucket without comparing against most other elements, which is structurally impossible for an unsorted list that has no index into its contents by value.

options.text: A hash-based set and an unsorted list have the same average membership-check cost, but the set simply uses less memory.
options.explanation: This denies the actual performance difference: an unsorted list's average membership-check cost is O(n), not equal to a hash-based set's average O(1), regardless of memory usage.
